title: Magia kernel design: what FreeBSD and Linux each do best
scope: x86_64 kernel only, written from scratch; FreeBSD 15.1 / freebsd-src main vs Linux 7.4.0-rc3 docs / torvalds/linux master

labels.Verified: stated in a primary source that was opened
labels.Reported: author/vendor measurement or report of statements

answer: Where Magia's plan has already decided, it takes the better-supported side: Capsicum, jails, kqueue, a typed sysctl tree and a master syscall table from FreeBSD; EEVDF and ring-based I/O from Linux. For parts not yet planned, the evidence favours blk-mq queues with GEOM-style layering, RCU path lookup, folio-style page units, VNET with one filter VM, DTrace-style static probes and the Linux/KSPP hardening baseline. Three changes to the existing plan are supported: narrow and gate the io_uring-style rings, keep resource accounting in one cgroup-v2-style hierarchy, and add the Linux hardening the plan lacks (strong stack protector, zero-initialised stacks, kCFI/IBT, later KASLR). Confidence: medium-high for the facts (primary sources, dated); the picks themselves are inference.

rows.subsystem: Process sandboxing: Capsicum vs seccomp-bpf / Landlock

freebsd.design: Capsicum (since 9.0): cap_enter(2) puts a process in capability mode, which cuts access to global namespaces (file-system paths, PIDs); each file descriptor carries rights limited with cap_rights_limit(2); process descriptors replace PIDs. Capability mode cannot be left and is inherited by children.
strengths: One deny-by-default model: rights travel with descriptors
Very little code to adopt (about 100 lines for Chromium in 2010)
Measured cost small: capability-aware syscalls a few percent slower (2010)
weaknesses: Programs must open what they need before entering capability mode (Inference)
The Linux port proposed in 2014 is not in mainline, so there is no cross-platform reuse (Inference)

linux.design: seccomp-bpf (filter mode since 3.5; seccomp() syscall since 3.17) runs a BPF filter on each syscall number and its register arguments. Landlock (since 5.13) lets an unprivileged process stack rulesets that restrict file-system access, TCP/UDP ports and some IPC scopes, with a versioned ABI.
strengths: seccomp filters apply to unmodified programs
Landlock is unprivileged and stackable; its ABI grows by numbered versions
weaknesses: seccomp filters cannot dereference pointers, so they cannot check paths; the kernel docs say filtering 'isn't a sandbox'
Three overlapping mechanisms (seccomp, Landlock, LSMs) (Inference)

magia_pick.text: Capsicum as the core sandbox: capability mode plus per-descriptor rights plus process descriptors. Mark each syscall as allowed or not in capability mode in the master syscall table, as FreeBSD's syscalls.master does with CAPENABLED. Borrow Landlock's numbered-ABI idea for adding new rights later. Leave seccomp-style filters out until Magia has a userland.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Magia has no legacy programs to keep working, which removes Capsicum's main cost (retrofitting). The model is simpler to reason about than a syscall filter and was cheap in the only measurement found.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Matches the plan (Rust 'Capsicum rights', FreeBSD errno ENOTCAPABLE/ECAPMODE).

rows.subsystem: Containers: jails vs namespaces + cgroups v2

freebsd.design: Jails (since 4.0): one kernel object per container with named parameters; hierarchical jails since 8.0; VNET jails get their own network stack. Resource limits via rctl(8) (since 9.0). The Handbook now also covers OCI containers with Podman.
strengths: One first-class object is easy to audit and name (Inference)
VNET gives each jail a full network stack
weaknesses: rctl write-bandwidth/IOPS limits are counted at the file-system cache, not the device

linux.design: Eight namespace types (cgroup, ipc, network, mount, pid, time, user, uts) combined per process; unprivileged user namespaces since 3.8. Resource control via cgroup v2, a single unified hierarchy.
strengths: Namespaces compose freely; cgroup v2's single tree replaced v1's multiple hierarchies, which 'wasn't useful in practice'
weaknesses: Unprivileged user namespaces became a step in several privilege-escalation chains; Ubuntu 23.10 restricted them
A 'container' is a userland convention over many kernel pieces (Inference)

magia_pick.text: A jail-like container object with VNET-style per-jail network stacks, plus one cgroup-v2-style hierarchy for resource accounting (controllers enabled per subtree). Do not add unprivileged user namespaces.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: The jail object keeps isolation in one place; cgroup v2 is the better-documented accounting model; the user-namespace record argues against unprivileged nesting.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Matches the plan ('jails + resource accounting'); suggests making the accounting hierarchical.

rows.subsystem: Event notification: kqueue vs epoll (and io_uring)

freebsd.design: kqueue/kevent (since 4.1): one call submits changes and collects events; filters cover READ, WRITE, AIO, VNODE, PROC, PROCDESC, SIGNAL, TIMER, USER, EMPTY, JAIL and JAILDESC.
strengths: Generic: one queue for fds, files, processes, signals, timers, user events and AIO completion
Kernel keeps the state, so cost does not grow with the number of watched objects per call (2001 design)
weaknesses: No source found on kqueue weaknesses at scale (Unknown)

linux.design: epoll: an interest list of file descriptors, edge- or level-triggered, scales to large numbers of descriptors. Non-fd events need fd wrappers (Inference: not checked here).
strengths: Well-known scaling for large fd sets
weaknesses: Interest is tied to the open file description: a closed fd that was dup'd keeps reporting events until all duplicates are closed

magia_pick.text: kqueue as Magia's single event queue, including a jail filter (FreeBSD 15.1's kqueue has JAIL and JAILDESC filters) and AIO/ring completions.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: One generic queue with typed filters is easier to secure and document than per-type descriptor wrappers.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Matches the plan (kqueue in the Rust crate).

claims.text: kqueue filters include READ, WRITE, AIO, VNODE, PROC, PROCDESC, SIGNAL, TIMER, USER, EMPTY, JAIL, JAILDESC; kqueue/kevent since FreeBSD 4.1; kqueuex() since 14.0.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: poll/select are stateless and O(N) per call; kqueue keeps state in the kernel and is generic beyond sockets and pipes.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: epoll scales to large numbers of fds; a closed fd that was duplicated keeps reporting events until all duplicates are closed.
claims.label: Verified

rows.subsystem: Asynchronous I/O: io_uring vs FreeBSD aio

freebsd.design: POSIX aio. Sockets, raw disks and local regular files are always truly asynchronous ('safe'); other file types are 'unsafe' and off by default (vfs.aio.enable_unsafe). Completions can be delivered through kqueue (EVFILT_AIO). aio_readv since 13.0, aio_read2 since 14.1.
strengths: Small, POSIX-defined surface; integrates with kqueue
weaknesses: Only some file types are truly async by default

linux.design: io_uring: submission and completion rings shared between user space and kernel, so many requests need no syscall each. A sysctl (kernel.io_uring_disabled, 0/1/2) can restrict or disable it.
strengths: Author's 2019 benchmark: 1.7M 4 KiB IOPS polled vs 608K with Linux native aio; about 1.2M non-polled
weaknesses: Google (2023): 60% of kCTF VRP exploit submissions in the prior year used io_uring; disabled on ChromeOS and production Google servers, blocked for Android apps

magia_pick.text: Keep the ring design for speed, but narrow it: a small fixed opcode set that reuses the normal syscall handlers and Capsicum rights checks, a sysctl kill switch like io_uring_disabled, and completions that can also be posted to kqueue.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Rings win on throughput, but io_uring's breadth made it the top exploit target in Google's programme; a narrow, rights-checked ring keeps most of the gain with less new surface (Inference).
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Plan has 'io_uring-style rings'; add the opcode allowlist and kill switch.

rows.subsystem: CPU scheduler: ULE vs CFS -> EEVDF, plus sched_ext

freebsd.design: ULE (since 5.1): per-CPU run queues, CPU affinity, topology and hyper-threading awareness, interactivity heuristics. FreeBSD 15 builds ULE and 4BSD together and picks one at boot (ULE default).
strengths: Per-CPU queues and locks from the start (2003 design)
Better long-run load balance than CFS in the 2018 study
weaknesses: ULE 'may cause starvation', even with identical threads (2018 study)

linux.design: EEVDF replaced CFS in 6.6 (2023-10-29): each task has lag and a virtual deadline; tasks may request a time slice via sched_setattr(). sched_ext (from 6.12, 2024-11-17) lets BPF programs implement a scheduler class that can be switched at runtime, with automatic fallback.
strengths: Deadlines give a defined latency knob per task
sched_ext allows experiments without risking the system: default restored on error, stall or SysRq-S
weaknesses: 2018 study: no overall winner over ULE; CFS-era data only (no ULE vs EEVDF study found)

magia_pick.text: EEVDF as the default policy, per-CPU run queues when Magia goes SMP, and a scheduler-class interface so a second policy can be chosen at boot (FreeBSD 15 style) and, later, loaded with a safety fallback (sched_ext idea).
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Measured evidence shows no overall winner, so pick the design with the clearest fairness and latency definition and keep it swappable.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Matches the plan (EEVDF in Rust; nice-to-weight table recomputed from its formula).

rows.subsystem: Kernel tunables: sysctl MIB tree vs /proc/sys + sysfs

freebsd.design: One sysctl MIB tree: numeric OIDs also addressable by name, typed values (integers, strings, tables), kernel-side registration with a description string per node, and per-node flags (e.g. which nodes are reachable in capability mode).
strengths: Typed, self-describing, one namespace
Per-node policy flags (capability mode allows about 60 of over 15,000 nodes)
weaknesses: No per-node stability level documented like Linux's ABI files (Inference)

linux.design: /proc/sys text files for tunables and sysfs for device/kernel objects ('one value per file', ASCII). The binary sysctl(2) syscall was removed in 5.5. Stability is documented per file in Documentation/ABI (stable, testing, obsolete, removed).
strengths: Plain files work with any tool; ABI stability levels are written down
weaknesses: Untyped text; two separate trees; binary interface removed

magia_pick.text: FreeBSD-style typed MIB with descriptions and per-node flags (read-only, boot tunable, capability-mode allowed), registered through linker sets; add a Linux-style stability level per node (stable/testing/obsolete).
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Typed nodes with flags serve both the sandbox and documentation; Linux's stability levels make the promise explicit.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Matches the plan (sysctl MIB tree in Rust, linker sets).

rows.subsystem: Storage layering: GEOM vs device-mapper / block layer

freebsd.design: GEOM: a modular framework of classes, geoms, providers and consumers that transform disk I/O requests; classes can stack in any order (only cycles are forbidden). Classes include ELI (encryption), MIRROR, RAID, PART_*, UZIP and GATE.
strengths: One uniform graph for every transformation; topology-agnostic and extensible
weaknesses: No current scaling measurement of GEOM found (Unknown)

linux.design: device-mapper targets (crypt, integrity, verity, thin, cache, raid, zoned, vdo, snapshot, linear, stripe, ...) on top of blk-mq, the multi-queue block layer with per-CPU software queues mapped to hardware queues.
strengths: blk-mq removed the single request-queue lock bottleneck and scaled to about 10 million IOPS (2013)
Broad set of production targets
weaknesses: No weakness documented in the sources read (Unknown)

magia_pick.text: A blk-mq-style per-CPU multi-queue core for submission, with GEOM-style providers and consumers for every transform (partitions, encryption, mirroring).
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: blk-mq has the measured scaling; GEOM has the cleaner composition model; they sit at different layers, so both fit.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Not yet in the plan (no block layer yet).

claims.label: Verified

claims.label: Verified

rows.subsystem: File systems and VFS: ZFS/UFS vs ext4/btrfs

freebsd.design: ZFS (OpenZFS): checksums on all data with self-repair from redundancy, pooled storage, ARC/L2ARC/ZIL. UFS with soft-updates journaling. VFS built on vnodes with use, hold and write counts; vnodes are recycled across file systems.
strengths: ZFS end-to-end checksums and self-healing in base
weaknesses: ZFS is CDDL: FreeBSD allows it only in modules, not the static kernel

linux.design: ext4 (mature default) and btrfs (RAID5/6 still 'unstable'). ZFS is not in mainline. VFS with a dentry cache and RCU-walk lockless path lookup, falling back to REF-walk.
strengths: RCU-walk path lookup avoids locks on the common path
weaknesses: btrfs RAID56 unstable (status page, 2026-10-16)
ZFS stays out of mainline over licensing (Torvalds, 2020)

magia_pick.text: Linux-style dentry cache with RCU-walk path lookup once Magia is SMP; when a disk file system is added, design it around ZFS-style checksums on every block, verified on read and repaired from redundancy. Keep ramfs/devfs for now.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Path lookup is the hottest VFS path and RCU-walk is documented in depth; end-to-end checksums are the main correctness gain ZFS shows.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Plan has VFS + ramfs + devfs + pipes; no disk file system yet.

rows.subsystem: Memory management: FreeBSD VM/UMA vs Linux SLUB/folios/MGLRU

freebsd.design: VM objects with shadow objects for copy-on-write, unified with the buffer cache. UMA zone allocator with per-CPU caches and NUMA policies. Reservation-based transparent superpages (since 7.2 on amd64/i386), enabled by default in the current amd64 pmap.
strengths: Superpages without a background collapse daemon: reservations promote pages in place (Inference from the design)
Reservation superpages gave gains 'often exceeding 30%' (2002)
weaknesses: VM complexity is driven by performance (Dillon)

linux.design: SLUB is the slab allocator (SLAB was removed in 6.8). Folios: a type for a page that is never a tail page, used to handle multi-page units cleanly. MGLRU: generation-based page reclaim. Transparent huge pages with always/madvise modes, khugepaged and multi-size THP.
strengths: MGLRU at Google: 40% less kswapd CPU, 85% fewer low-memory kills (p75), 18% better app launch
Folios: clearer types; 7% faster kernel builds reported from related page-cache work
weaknesses: Folio conversion is a multi-year retrofit (Inference)

magia_pick.text: Keep the plan's buddy allocator, struct page array and slab zones; give zones per-CPU caches (UMA/SLUB style) when SMP arrives; use a folio-like multi-page type in the page cache from day one; FreeBSD-style reservation superpages for anonymous memory; generation-based (MGLRU-like) reclaim later.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Folio-style typing is cheap in a new kernel and expensive to retrofit; reservations get superpages without a scanning daemon; MGLRU has the best measured reclaim data.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Plan has buddy + struct page + slab zones and a single address space for now.

rows.subsystem: Networking: netgraph, VNET, pf vs nftables, XDP/eBPF

freebsd.design: netgraph: graphs of nodes and hooks that supplement the stack. VNET: several isolated network stacks in one kernel, attached to jails. pf (from OpenBSD 4.5, reworked for multi-CPU) alongside IPFW and IPFILTER. netmap fast packet I/O in base.
strengths: VNET makes per-container stacks a kernel feature (2003 design)
netmap: 14.88 Mpps on one 900 MHz core (2012)
weaknesses: Three firewalls in base, each with its own syntax

linux.design: nftables: an in-kernel virtual machine for rules, with sets, maps and incremental updates, replacing protocol-specific iptables code. XDP: eBPF programs at the driver hook, checked by the eBPF verifier.
strengths: XDP up to 24 Mpps per core while keeping the kernel's security boundary (2018)
nftables: new protocols often need no new kernel code
weaknesses: XDP peak below DPDK (2018)
Unprivileged BPF can be switched off, and a build option makes that the default

magia_pick.text: VNET-style stack instances from the start (one per jail); one packet filter built on a small rule VM with sets and maps (nftables idea) instead of several firewalls; an XDP-like early hook later that shares the verifier with tracing.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Per-jail stacks fit the container model; one VM plus one verifier is less code than several filter engines (Inference).
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Not yet in the plan (no network stack yet).

freebsd.design: DTrace: providers expose probes that cost nothing when disabled; D scripts run with safety guarantees. FreeBSD has full kernel DTrace (userland is experimental) and, since 14.0, kinst (probe any instruction in a kernel function).
strengths: 'Zero probe effect' when disabled and a safety-first design (2004)
A mature language (D) and probe naming
weaknesses: Userland DTrace on FreeBSD is experimental

linux.design: ftrace: function tracer and latency tracers; dynamic ftrace turns mcount/fentry call sites into NOPs at boot and patches them back when enabled. eBPF programs, checked by the verifier, attach to probes; bpftrace offers a DTrace-like language. Oracle maintains a Linux DTrace built on BPF.
strengths: One verified bytecode serves tracing, networking and scheduling (sched_ext)
ftrace is near-zero cost when off
weaknesses: The verifier is a large, complex component (Inference)

magia_pick.text: Static probe points (DTrace SDT style) registered through linker sets now; NOP-patched function-entry hooks (ftrace style) later; one small verified bytecode VM for probe actions, shared with the packet filter.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Static probes are cheap to add while the code is young; a single verified VM serves several subsystems, as eBPF shows.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Plan already uses linker sets; tracing not yet planned.

freebsd.design: One master file (syscalls.master) generates the syscall tables; COMPAT4..COMPAT15 entries compiled under COMPAT_FREEBSDx options keep old binaries running; a CAPENABLED flag per syscall. Syscall man pages live in the source tree.
strengths: Single source of truth for the syscall table
Explicit compatibility shims per old release
Docs maintained next to the code (219 section-2 pages in lib/libsys)
weaknesses: Compatibility promise is per stable branch; old ABIs need compile-time COMPAT options

linux.design: 'We don't cause regressions' is the first rule: userland interfaces (syscalls, procfs, sysfs) must keep working; in-kernel APIs are deliberately unstable. Documentation/ABI marks interfaces stable/testing/obsolete/removed. Syscall man pages are a separate project.
strengths: Strongest userland promise: applications keep working across releases
Freedom to rework internal APIs (USB reworked at least three times)
weaknesses: No stable module API: out-of-tree drivers break
Syscall docs live outside the kernel tree

magia_pick.text: One master syscall table that generates dispatch, typed argument validation, capability flags and a doc stub; man pages in the Magia tree; a per-ABI personality table so a compatibility ABI can be added later; adopt Linux's 'never break userspace' promise once Magia has users; keep internal APIs unstable.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: FreeBSD's generator removes drift between table, checks and docs; Linux's rule is the clearest user promise but costs more once made, so make it when there are users.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Plan has a 'syscall table with typed argument validation' and Linux-style negative errno returns.

claims.text: 'We don't cause regressions' is the first rule of Linux kernel development; it covers procfs, sysfs and other userland interfaces but not kernel-internal interfaces such as the module API.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Linux has no stable in-kernel API or binary interface by design; the syscall interface 'is very stable over time, and will not break'; in-kernel USB interfaces were reworked at least three times.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Documentation/ABI stable interfaces are guaranteed at least 2 years; syscalls are expected never to change.
claims.label: Verified

rows.subsystem: License: BSD-2-Clause vs GPLv2 and the effect on reuse

freebsd.design: BSD-2-Clause for the compilation and for new code; the static GENERIC kernel must be BSD-licensed or similar; GPL, APSL and CDDL code is allowed only in loadable modules (CDDL approved for DTrace and ZFS).
strengths: Permissive: code can be reused in almost any project with notices kept
weaknesses: No obligation for downstream users to share changes (Inference)

linux.design: GPL-2.0-only with the syscall note: programs that only use syscalls are not derived works. Individual files may be GPL-compatible or dual-licensed (e.g. GPL plus BSD or MIT). Every file carries an SPDX identifier.
strengths: Copyleft keeps derived kernels open (Inference)
Syscall note keeps user programs free of GPL obligations
weaknesses: GPL-2.0-only code cannot be copied into a BSD-licensed kernel

magia_pick.text: Keep Magia's BSD-2-Clause licence, add an SPDX line to every file (both projects use SPDX), and keep the documented clean-room rule (ideas only, no copied code). If code is ever imported, only BSD/MIT-licensed code or the permissive side of dual-licensed Linux files is compatible.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: BSD-2 matches FreeBSD's policy and keeps every FreeBSD idea and permissively licensed driver reusable; GPL-only Linux code would force a licence change. Legal reading, not legal advice.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Magia's LICENSE is BSD 2-Clause; the plan forbids copying code from Linux or FreeBSD.

claims.text: Linux is GPL-2.0-only with an explicit syscall exception; files may be dual-licensed with BSD or MIT; SPDX identifiers are required.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Syscall note: user programs using kernel services by normal system calls are not 'derived work'; only GPL v2 is valid.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: FreeBSD's compilation is under BSD-2 terms (Copyright 1992-2026 The FreeBSD Project).
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: New FreeBSD code should use BSD-2-Clause; 'GPL, APSL, CDDL, etc, licensed software must not be compiled into the static GENERIC kernel'; allowed in pre-compiled modules; CDDL approved for DTrace and ZFS.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Linux iwlwifi and rtw89 are 'GPL-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause'; i915 and amdgpu carry MIT permission text; nvme host core is 'GPL-2.0'.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Magia is BSD 2-Clause and its plan forbids copying code from Linux or FreeBSD.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: A BSD-2 kernel may import BSD/MIT code and the permissive side of dual-licensed files, but not GPL-2.0-only code without relicensing (not legal advice).
claims.label: Inference

freebsd.design: Native drivers in sys/dev plus Linux drivers run through the LinuxKPI compatibility layer: Wi-Fi (iwlwifi, rtw88, rtw89; mt76 in progress) in sys/contrib/dev, and AMD/Intel GPU drivers ported one Linux version at a time in drm-kmod (ports). The FreeBSD Foundation funds a laptop-support project.
strengths: LinuxKPI reuses permissively licensed Linux drivers 'mostly unmodified'
weaknesses: Lag and gaps: DRM drivers at Linux 6.12 LTS for FreeBSD 15.1 (Q2 2026); ath11k/ath12k TODO and brcmfmac missing shims (Q1 2026)

linux.design: Drivers are kept in-tree and are fixed together with internal API changes; drivers/ is about 70% of the source tree by bytes.
strengths: Largest driver set; in-tree drivers stay working when APIs change
weaknesses: Out-of-tree drivers get no stable API

magia_pick.text: Do not chase breadth: target QEMU's virtual devices first (virtio), then a few common real devices; keep drivers in-tree with an unstable internal API; shape the driver interfaces so a LinuxKPI-like shim could host permissively licensed Linux drivers later, if the no-copy rule is ever relaxed.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Even FreeBSD relies on Linux for GPU and Wi-Fi drivers; a hobby kernel cannot close that gap by writing drivers alone.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Plan covers serial, VGA, PIC and PIT only.

rows.subsystem: Security mitigations: KASLR, SMEP/SMAP, CFI, stack protector, W^X

freebsd.design: Userland ASLR, PIE, W^X policy and PROT_MAX; RELRO; stack protector (kernel built with -fstack-protector and one global canary on amd64); SMAP and SMEP used automatically on amd64; per-vulnerability hardware mitigation sysctls. No KASLR; kernel CFI not committed.
strengths: Simple, documented per-process controls (proccontrol, sysctl)
weaknesses: No KASLR (bug report, 2026-05-23)
kCFI review accepted 2026-06-03 but not in main as of 2026-11-20

linux.design: Kernel text and read-only data never writable (STRICT_KERNEL_RWX since 4.11), __ro_after_init, SMEP/SMAP, stack protector (strong), KASLR for kernel and modules, structure-layout randomisation, zero-initialised stacks, hardened usercopy, IBT and kCFI/FineIBT, page-table isolation, kernel-stack erasing (KSPP list).
strengths: Broadest kernel self-protection set, with a maintained recommended configuration
weaknesses: Many options are build-time choices; defaults vary by distribution (Inference)

magia_pick.text: Linux/KSPP as the baseline. Magia's plan already has NX/WP/SMEP/SMAP, W^X kernel mappings and stack canaries at thread-stack bottoms. Add next: compiler stack protector (strong) and zero-initialised stack variables for the C code, guard pages for kernel stacks, hardened copyin/copyout, Clang kCFI plus IBT for C; KASLR once the kernel can relocate (it is linked at a fixed higher-half address).
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Hardening is cheapest before code grows; Linux's list is documented and measured in production; FreeBSD lacks KASLR and kernel CFI.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Partly in the plan (NX/WP/SMEP/SMAP, W^X, stack canaries, SMAP-aware copyin/copyout).

claims.text: FreeBSD mitigations(7) lists ASLR/PIE, W^X (allow_wx), PROT_MAX, RELRO, SSP (kernel -fstack-protector, single global canary except aarch64 option), FORTIFY_SOURCE, SMAP/SMEP automatic on amd64, Capsicum; no KASLR or kernel CFI entry.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Bug 295522 (2026-05-23) states 'FreeBSD does not implement KASLR'.
claims.label: Reported

claims.text: amd64 FreeBSD kernels can load anywhere in the lower 4 GB physically since 2025-06 (relocation, not randomisation).
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: FreeBSD kCFI review D46193 was accepted on 2026-06-03, but main has no KCFI build option and commit search finds no 'kcfi' commit (2026-11-20).
claims.label: Inference

claims.text: Linux self-protection: executable code and read-only data must not be writable; __ro_after_init; SMEP/SMAP; stack canary; KASLR of kernel and module base; structure layout randomisation; memory initialisation.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: KSPP recommends STRICT_KERNEL_RWX (since 4.11), STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG, HARDENED_USERCOPY, INIT_STACK_ALL_ZERO, RANDOMIZE_BASE, X86_KERNEL_IBT, CFI_CLANG, PAGE_TABLE_ISOLATION, RANDSTRUCT_FULL, ZERO_CALL_USED_REGS, KSTACK_ERASE (since 6.17).
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Magia plan: NX/WP/SMEP/SMAP, W^X layout, stack canaries at stack bottoms, SMAP-aware copyin/copyout; kernel linked at 0xffffffff80000000.
claims.label: Verified

rows.subsystem: Rust in each kernel: where it is used and why

freebsd.design: No Rust in the kernel tree. A 2025 proof of concept builds optional Rust userland programs ('We do NOT currently support Rust in the kernel'). Out of tree, a Rust kernel programming interface (KPI) with a virtio-sound driver and Apple M2 drivers is in development (x86-64 and aarch64 only; interfaces not yet stable). The 2024 debate stalled on build cost and missing build integration.
strengths: Rust KPI avoids external crates and allocating std parts, aiming for C-like stability
weaknesses: No in-tree kernel Rust; 2024 estimate that Rust in base would 'double our build times'

linux.design: Rust support merged in 6.1 as an experiment, declared concluded at the 2025 Maintainers Summit ('Rust is here to stay'). Mainline Rust users include the Android Binder driver (6.18), parts of the Nova NVIDIA driver, the Tyr GPU driver, rnull, two PHY drivers and the DRM panic QR generator; Android 16 ships Rust ashmem. Drivers must use safe subsystem abstractions, not raw C bindings. The first CVE in Rust kernel code (CVE-2025-68260, Binder) was a race in an unsafe block.
strengths: Production use on millions of Android devices
Maintainers report Rust drivers 'far safer'; 41% of C null_blk fixes were memory-safety fixes
weaknesses: Mixed-language toolchain cost; not all architectures/configurations work
unsafe blocks still produce CVEs

magia_pick.text: Keep the plan's split: C for boot, CPU, MMU and context switch; a no_std Rust crate with zero external dependencies for policy subsystems. Confine unsafe code and FFI to one module that exposes safe abstractions (Linux's rule), require a written safety argument for every unsafe block, and pin the toolchain.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: The reason both projects give for Rust is memory safety, not speed; Linux's experience shows the gain comes from safe abstractions and that remaining bugs cluster in unsafe code.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Matches the plan (rust/ crate, stable toolchain, x86_64-unknown-none, 'ffi + kenv').

claims.text: Rust support was merged in v6.1 as an experiment; at the 2025 Maintainers Summit the experiment was deemed concluded: 'Rust is here to stay'; not everything works for every configuration, architecture or toolchain.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Nova pieces merged; Binder merged for 6.18; Android 16 on 6.12 ships Rust ashmem; Rust code grew about fivefold in a year; DRM maintainer: 'about a year away' from requiring Rust for new drivers; Kroah-Hartman: Rust drivers 'proving to be far safer'.
claims.label: Reported

claims.text: Rust users in mainline: AMCC QT2025 PHY, Android Binder, ASIX PHY, DRM panic QR generator, Nova, rnull, Tyr; outside mainline: ashmem, Apple AGX, NVMe, PuzzleFS. Each subsystem decides whether to take Rust.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Drivers should not use C bindings directly; subsystems provide safe abstractions.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: CVE-2025-68260 (published 2025-12-16): race condition in an unsafe list removal in Rust Binder.
claims.label: Verified

claims.label: Reported

claims.text: Android: memory-safety share of vulnerabilities fell from 76% to 24% over six years as new code moved to memory-safe languages (mostly userland code).
claims.label: Reported

claims.label: Verified

claims.label: Verified

rows.subsystem: C vs Rust performance in kernel code

linux.design: Three sources measure Rust kernel drivers against C: a peer-reviewed study (2024), the Rust-for-Linux maintainers' own benchmarks (2025 rebases), and a master's thesis (2025).
strengths: Mature, feature-matched Rust drivers are within about +/-3% (NVMe) and -5% to +15% (null block) of C in maintainers' benchmarks
weaknesses: 2024 study: up to 61% slower or 67% faster by configuration; e1000 11x slower ping latency (missing features); binaries 1.2x-2.4x larger
Thesis: GPIO module 8-14% slower and 28-46% more energy

magia_pick.text: Speed is not a reason against Rust in Magia. Watch the known costs: binary size, bounds checks in hot loops, coarse locks and emulated bit fields. Magia's single Giant lock is fine for uniprocessor but should become finer-grained locks before SMP.
magia_pick.label: Inference
magia_pick.why: Where the Rust and C drivers implement the same features, the measured gap is small; the large gaps traced to missing features or coarse locking.
magia_pick.fit_with_plan: Plan: uniprocessor, one Giant lock around Rust subsystem state.

claims.text: ATC 2024: Rust drivers 'on par' with C 'within a 20% gap'; e1000 11x slower ping latency (lacks features such as prefetch); Binder about 10% latency gap; NVMe/null block from 61% degradation to 67% improvement by setting; binaries 1.2x (binder) to 2.4x (gpio) larger; causes: coarse locks, bounds checks, emulated bit fields, pointer-heavy ownership.
claims.label: Verified

claims.text: Rust NVMe driver (v6.15 rebase): (R-C)/C between about -3% and +3% for random reads on one core (Ryzen 5 7600, Samsung 990 Pro); the driver is 'not currently suitable for general use'. Values read from the plot.
claims.label: Reported

claims.text: rnull (v6.19-rc5): IOPS difference vs C mostly between -5% and +15% across block sizes and queue depths; authors warn earlier results may mislead because distributions were not normal. Values read from the plot.
claims.label: Reported

claims.text: Thesis (Raspberry Pi 4 GPIO module): Rust +8%, +11%, +14.3% execution time and +46.15%, +27.68%, +33.86% energy across three variants.
claims.label: Reported

claims.text: Magia plan: uniprocessor with one Giant IRQ-disabling lock plus a scheduler lock.
claims.label: Verified

conflicts.topic: First CVE in Rust kernel code
conflicts.a: LWN, 2025-12-13 [S96]: Kroah-Hartman said no CVE had yet been issued for Rust code.
conflicts.b: NVD, 2025-12-16 [S100]: CVE-2025-68260 published for Rust Binder.
conflicts.weight: Both were true on their dates; NVD is newer and primary, so the current fact is: one CVE exists, in an unsafe block.

conflicts.topic: How fast Rust kernel drivers are versus C
conflicts.a: ATC 2024 [S103]: usually within 20%, but -61% to +67% by setting and e1000 11x slower.
conflicts.b: Rust-for-Linux maintainers, 2025 rebases [S101, S102]: NVMe within about +/-3%, rnull -5% to +15%. Thesis 2025 [S104]: GPIO 8-14% slower.
conflicts.weight: I weight the maintainers' newer, feature-matched benchmarks most for 'can Rust match C' (they have confidence intervals), while noting they are the authors' own numbers. ATC 2024 is peer-reviewed but measured older drivers with missing features; the thesis is one small driver.

conflicts.a: Capsicum paper, 2010-08 [S3]: Linux Chromium sandbox 11,301 lines vs about 100 with Capsicum.
conflicts.b: seccomp filter mode arrived in Linux 3.5 [S5], after the paper; Landlock in 5.13 [S6].
conflicts.weight: Treat the line counts as historical; they compare with seccomp strict mode, not today's seccomp-bpf or Landlock.

conflicts.a: Axboe, 2019 [S18]: rings give about 2.8x the IOPS of Linux aio (author's benchmark).
conflicts.b: Google, 2023-06-14 [S22] and Linux sysctl docs [S23]: io_uring was the top exploit target and can be disabled.
conflicts.weight: Not a contradiction but a trade-off; both are primary for their own claims. The Magia pick keeps rings but narrows them.

conflicts.a: Bouron et al., 2018-07 [S26]: no overall winner between ULE and CFS.
conflicts.b: Linux replaced CFS with EEVDF in 6.6, 2023-10-29 [S30].
conflicts.weight: The only head-to-head study predates EEVDF; no ULE-vs-EEVDF comparison was found, so the current answer is Unknown.

conflicts.a: Commit 2025-06-22 [S90]: amd64 kernels are now physically relocatable.
conflicts.weight: Relocation is a prerequisite, not randomisation; I weight the 2026 bug report and the man page: FreeBSD has no KASLR.

would_change: Magia needs to run Linux binaries: FreeBSD's multi-ABI design (one kernel, several userland ABIs) moves from 'later' to 'core' [S83].
The no-copy rule is relaxed or the licence becomes GPL-2.0: driver and file-system picks change, because Linux code could then be imported [S78, S81].
Magia goes SMP: per-CPU run queues, RCU-walk path lookup, per-CPU allocator caches and finer locks become urgent rather than later [S49, S53, S103].
A published ULE-vs-EEVDF benchmark appears: the scheduler pick could change [S26].
FreeBSD commits kernel CFI or KASLR, or Linux DRM starts requiring Rust for new drivers (stated as about a year away in Dec 2025): the mitigation and Rust comparisons would need updating [S91, S96].
The project prefers fewer languages: a C-only core changes the Rust row; the evidence then supports C with KSPP-style hardening [S88].
not_verified: The 2018 ULE vs CFS paper: only the abstract page was read; the PDF refused automated download (HTTP 403).
Rust-for-Linux benchmark values were read by eye from the SVG plots (rendered locally), not from raw data.
FreeBSD kernel CFI 'not committed' is inferred from absence: no KCFI option in main's sys/conf files and no commit-search hit for 'kcfi' on 2026-11-20.
No published ULE-vs-EEVDF comparison and no kqueue-vs-epoll benchmark were found or run.
FreeBSD's own lockless path-lookup work was not checked.
Driver breadth is measured in source bytes, not supported devices; generated register headers inflate Linux's count.
Google's Android memory-safety data is mostly userland code; applying it to kernel code is inference.
The LWN Rust session report relays statements made in a meeting (labelled Reported).
ZFS licensing: Torvalds' view is an opinion, not a court ruling. All licence readings here are not legal advice.
kernel.org docs, the nftables wiki and some FreeBSD docs show no page date; the HTTP Last-Modified date is given instead.
Whether Clang kCFI can cover Magia's Rust code was not checked.
